I really dig Rohmer too, here are some of the closest to his style that I can think of.

Linklater’s Before Trilogy. 

Some of Hamaguchi’s films like Wheel of Fortune and Fantasy, Asako I & 2, Happy Hour.

Hong Sang-soo entire filmography.

Hong Sang-soo is often compared to Rohmer, though I’m not sure I would call the dialogue poetic. Some of my favorites are: On the Beach at Night Alone; Right Now, Wrong Then; Tale of Cinema; Claire’s Camera; On the Occassion of Remembering the Turning Gate
Thanks!
Thanks!
Or probably Arnaud Desplechin. He's actually to far from Rohmer but if you like these relationships and identity conflicts of white bourgeois parisian people that would come close to Rohmer.

I confirm excellent choice, notably the masterful Kings and Queen

Some of Truffaut's films e.g. 'Jules et Jim' and 'Two English Girls' sort of fit this bill, but they're a bit more 'cinematic' and a bit less 'writerly' than Rohmer's stuff.

Jacques Rivette's stuff kind of fits the bill too, especially 'La Belle Noiseuse'.
[removed]

From last year, you might like Christian Petzold’s Afire. I’m pretty sure he said he made it after binging Rohmer during quarantine lol. Really amazing film about two friends who go to a seaside cabin for vacation.

His good friend Rivette (though he's much more surreal, there are many long scenes of people just interacting that feel like they could be in a Rohmer movie; and Rivette himself, with an outrageously fake beard, plays a Balzac scholar in *Out 1*).

Olivier Assayas, maybe. Try *Summer Hours* or *Non-fiction*.
[removed]
[removed]
Yeah, La Belle Noiseuse by Rivette fits the bill!

I think the closest are *Va Savoir* (translated as *Who Knows?* or *Go Figure*), *Gang of Four*, *Up Down Fragile*, and sections of *Out 1.* I must admit that *La Belle Noiseuse* it pretty far down in my Rivette rankings, so it wouldn't be my first recommendation.
And Un conte de Noël (A Christmas Tale)

Yeah I’ve watched decent amount of Rivettes films and La Belle Noiseuse is great and definitely has the feeling of a Rohmer film.

General rule of thumb, if there’s a scene where people have thoughtful conversations while sitting in the sun on patio furniture, they probably like Rohmer.

Damn, good reminder that I finally should start watching Rohmer! But based on your preferences I recommend Louis Malle's Le Feu Follet (The Fire Within). It's sad and beautiful, I recommend it whenever I get the chance.

I liked the dialogue in L'Avenir (Things to Come) by Mia Hansen-Løve, it focuses more on philosophy in an unpretentious way - and features Isabelle Huppert. 

What is it with the French and their majectic talkiness...?!

Although you should check out Nuri Bilge Ceylan's work too, for instance  Once Upon a Time in Anatolia, if you like silence and beautiful cinematography in between the lengthy conversations.
Thanks, I really need to catch up...
The Before trilogy is basically my favourite thing in cinema but I’ve never heard of Rohmer.
And Comment je me suis disputé... (Ma vie sexuelle)

Rohmer was one of the somewhat lesser know directors of the French New Wave. He has a ton of great films and yeah if you dig the Before Trilogy you'll almost definitely get something out of them. Though I would note that his films made in the 80s and 90s have more in common with what Linklater did in the BT than his earlier films (which are still great btw).  Check out any of these and you'll probably have a good time: 

The Green Ray, A Summer’s Tale, Pauline at the Beach, Boyfriends and Girlfriends, The Aviator’s Wife

Definitely Guillaume Brac. Check out *All Hands on Deck* *July Tales* and *A World Without Women*. He is very very obviously trying to emulate Rohmer's style (but imo it somehow doesn't come across as annoying or cringey that he is doing so since the characters do feel authentic).

Nicolas Pariser's *Alice and the Mayor*. Heavy focus on dialogue and with its combination of Fabrice Luchini and mayoral politics it seems like a sort of updating of Rohmer's *The Tree, the Mayor, and the Mediatheque*.

Ted Fendt's *Outside Noise*. Relies a lot on people walking around having philosophical conversations.

Maybe Mikhael Hers - particularly *This Summer Feeling*, *Memory Lane* and *Primrose Hill* - though he uses music a lot lot more than Rohmer.

Could also check out the recent Spanish film *Girlfriends and Girlfriends*. Wasn't really as Rohmer-esque as I was expecting given the title but does feature people discussing his films and going to see them.

You should check out Dan Sallit. I went to a screening of *The Unspeakable Act* and afterwards there was a discussion with him, and he listed Rohmer as a direct influence, which was pretty evident in his work. He’s a great indie director and has made some awesome stuff- highly recommend checking him out

In addition to the excellent previous suggestions, I would suggest films by Emmanuel Mouret, preferably those in which he doesn't star (he's not a fantastic actor to say the least). Maybe those with Vincent Macaigne ?

*Afire* is fantastic.

Oh, Afire has been in my queue ever since it got on the Criterion Channel, and finding out that it was inspired by a Rohmer binge makes me very intrigued. 

I was a bit worried it was going to be depressing because the main dude in the preview seems a bit of a sad-sack. I don't love movies that begin and end in a space of clinical depression, so would you describe the overall mood of Afire as a bummer?
[removed]
I found A Christmas Tale kind of depressing.

Oh wow you just reduced what I am looking for in a movie and, who am I kidding, in life -- and I *think*  I am OK with that as my ideal. Maybe you should come over to my patio and we can discuss it for 6 to 12 hours.

Not quite. It's less depression, more that the dude in the preview is a bit of a pretentious hack and the movie is an almost satire about how far certain writer's pretensions go. The ending can be seen as a downer. But I would not say the mood of Afire is sustained melancholy or depression, it's a little lighter.

I second Hong Sang-soo. I haven't seen one of his films in a long time, but I recall really enjoying Woman is the Future of Man. 

Claire's Knee and Call Me By Your Name have some pretty clear aesthetic and thematic comparisons that I enjoyed. I put off watching the latter for a really long time because I'm an edgelord who actively avoids hyped things (this is a fault, not a feature), but when I finally did, I was pleasantly surprised.

Another mention for Hong Sang-soo. My personal favorites from him are "On the Occasion..." and "Right Now, Wrong Then".

Rivette definitely. 

Eugene Green is another director that I think you might enjoy. His approach to directing actors is much more formalist/artificial compared to Rohmer's naturalism but very sensitive and dialog-driven. My favorites from him are "The Bridge of Arts" and "Toutes les nuits".

I'm looking forward to seeing more from directors from the Diagonale collective but Vecchiali's "Rosa la rose, la fille publique" and Guiguet's "Faubourg St Martin" were wonderful and quite Rohmerian.

Robert Bresson's "Four Nights of a Dreamer" is the most Rohmer-like of all his films.
